title: Real-Time Software-Hardware Integration for Dynamic Control of Tissue Mechanical Environments
text: Mechanical forces control the way tissues respond to drugs, but current tools used by the scientific community to screen for new drugs do not incorporate these forces. We propose to integrate together new computational methods developed to calculate tissue forces, new materials that can change the forces they apply to cells in response to magnetic fields, and tools to accelerate computing to create systems in which forces produced by tissues can be measured in real-time, and this information can be applied to feedback and control the forces exerted on the tissue. The resulting integrated platform will allow scientists to perform drug screens in a more realistic environment to improve the ability to translate findings from drug screens to the clinic.

title: Chemosensory influences of intranasal cocaine on the reward system
text:
Chemosensory perception powerfully influences motivated behaviors. Intranasal cocaine evokes a nasal
sensory experience which likely contributes to cocaine’s reinforcing effects. The results from this work will
enhance our understanding of the mechanisms of nasal chemosensation and the effects of intranasal cocaine
on brain and behavior.

title: Revealing cancer metabolism via mass spectrometry and isotope tracers
text:
Metabolism plays a fundamental role in cancer growth, diagnosis, and treatment. I propose to develop improved
metabolomics, isotope tracing and imaging mass spectrometry technologies for quantitation of cancer metabolism, and
to apply the technology to reveal tumor metabolic activity. The resulting understanding of metabolite levels and fluxes
in cancer will open new therapeutic and diagnostic opportunities.

title: Epigenetic Regulation in Aging and Alzheimer's Disease
text:
The Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease, and the age is a major factor for
the most case of AD, but the mechanisms underlying the link between age and AD is still unclear. In this
project we will use mouse models and human postmortem tissue to examine a novel epigenetic mechanism
that effects on aging and AD, and whether changes of epigenetic regulation in aging could steer normal aging
toward AD development. The information derived from the project will help to develop new prevention and
treatment strategies that benefit AD patients.

title: Targeting the Cancer Stem Cells in Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor
text:
Nerve enriched environment and stem cell origin lead to the growth of the malignant peripheral nerve sheath
tumor (MPNST) and promote metastasis. NRG1, ERBB3, and CD44, the three essential genes, typically
regulate Schwan cell differentiation in the early developmental stage but form a positive feedback loop to
stimulate MPNST tumorigenesis and metastasis. Our work is expected to characterize the interactions and
regulations among them and evaluate the therapeutic value by interrupting the feedback loop and ultimately
inhibit tumor growth and metastasis.

title: Enabling improved applicability and transferability of polygenic scores across populations
text: FFAIRR-PRS will enhance the accuracy, generalizability, and clinical implementation of PRS, leading to earlier risk stratification. These advances will enhance public health by informing more personalized approaches to screening, treatment, and intervention.

title: Discovery of SARS-CoV-2 antivirals using a replicon assay
text:
We have developed a non-infectious, self-replicative SARS-CoV-2 replicon system that is a safe and effective
tool for antiviral screening and amenable to genetic engineering for studying drug resistance. We have identified
a small molecule inhibitor of SARS-CoV-2 antiviral activity, and early medicinal chemistry efforts have optimized
this lead. This project aims to further identify and characterize compounds toward the development of novel
inhibitors against SARS-CoV-2 with potent, nanomolar antiviral activity.

title: Molecular regulation of double-strand break repair by MDC1
text:
DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) pose critical threats to genomic integrity and stability. One critical protein that
facilitates DNA DSB repair is the DNA damage response protein, MDC1. These studies will reveal a new model
for how DSB repair is regulated by MDC1 which will provide critical insights into how genome integrity is
maintained in human cells.

title: Project 2. Immune evasion, trafficking, and nuclear import
text: Project 2 – Immune evasion, trafficking and nuclear import The HIV-1 capsid acts as the primary interface between the virus and the cell during viral ingress and nuclear entry. The capsid is critically involved throughout all steps of the replication cycle, including uncoating, recognition by host factors, trafficking along microtubules, nuclear import, and genome integration. Recent research revealed that HIV-1 capsid hijacks microtubule motors dynein and kinesin for its journey towards the nucleus, and an intact capsid can traverse the cellular nuclear pore complex (NPC). These data significantly impact our views of HIV-1 cytoplasmic transport, nuclear import, intranuclear transport, and uncoating, and indicate that capsid is a key player in HIV-1 ingress. However, atomic-level understanding of capsid recognition by host factors is lacking, and it is unclear how the dynamic exchange of factors occurs during viral movement from the cell periphery to the site of integration inside the nucleus. The overall goal of this project is to fill these knowledge gaps by providing critical structural and dynamic information on capsid’s engagement in immune evasion, trafficking and integration. The proposed studies are an integrated effort from seven PCHPI investigators and four cores (CryoEM/ET, NMR, Computational, and HIV Virology). Specifically, we will i) elucidate the interactions of HIV-1 capsid with host innate immune proteins, including MxB and TRIM5α/TRIMCyp; ii) determine the interactions between HIV-1 capsid and intracellular trafficking proteins, including kinesin-1/FEZ1 and dynein/dynactin/BICD2, and microtubules; and iii) define the dynamics of HIV-1 capsid interactions with host dependency factors involved in nuclear import, including the nucleoporins Nup358 and Nup153 and the host factors CPSF6 and SUN1/2. Our results will provide unprecedented atomic-level structural and dynamic view of capsid’s interactions with host proteins and could guide the development of new clinically relevant capsid inhibitors.

title: Mechanism and Function of XIST in X Chromosome Inactivation Maintenance
text:
Female-biased autoimmune diseases are inherently linked to the unbalanced X chromosome dosage between
sexes, potentially due to the defect of X-inactivation maintenance. This study will investigate the molecular
mechanism and function of lncRNA XIST in maintaining X-inactivation particularly in immune cells. Completion
of this study will provide mechanistic insights in the role of X-inactivation maintenance in sex dimorphism, and
shed light on potential therapeutic strategies to female-biased diseases.

title: Digital Tools for Precision Nephrology
text:
The proposal aims to establish robust phenotyping pipelines for early detection of Collagen Type IV-Associated
Nephropathy (COL4A-AN) using electronic health record (EHR) data. To overcome diagnostic challenges of
this prevalent monogenic form of chronic kidney disease (CKD), the study focuses on utilizing Natural
Language Processing (NLP) to extract nuanced phenotypic traits from unstructured clinical narratives and build
accurate and portable prediction models. These models lay the foundation for developing effective EHR-based
decision support tools that enable clinicians to identify patients with genetic CKD subtypes, even when
unfamiliar with specific genetic syndromes.

title: Enhanced treatment of breast cancer via biodegradable polymer nanoparticles
text:
Despite advances in the treatment of breast cancer, a significant number of tumors grow back, which can lead
to the need for more treatments or mortality. We herein propose to develop a new drug treatment that, when
combined with laser irradiation, should better prevent tumor recurrence and result in better outcomes for patients.

title: 3D Cine Magnetic Resonance Fingerprinting for Rapid Phenotyping of Cardiomyopathy
text:
We propose a novel 3D cine MR Fingerprinting exam for comprehensive characterization of cardiomyopathy
phenotypes, with prospective validation in patients. This research will streamline MRI exams, reduce operator
dependence, and provide reproducible quantitative tools for rapid and objective diagnosis of cardiomyopathies.

title: Vascular Toxicity of Benzene
text:
Benzene is a ubiquitous environmental pollutant and a known hematopoietic toxin but
little is known about the effect of benzene exposure on cardiovascular disease. The proposed
study will examine the effect of benzene exposure on atherosclerosis, the underlying cause of
most cardiovascular disease and stroke, and delineate the associated molecular mechanisms.

title: Training in Structural, Physiologic and Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging
text:
The complexity of MRI with its multiparametric nature and myriad embodiments for the study of tissue structure,
physiology and function, along with the increasing role of AI for image reconstruction and post processing,
requires systematic, modality-specific training. The proposed program entails all aspects of training physics and
engineering concepts for MRI image acquisition, processing and clinical translation, in combination with
preceptor-directed research.

title: High-Performance Multi-GPU System for Advanced Medical Imaging
text:
We propose a high-performance multi-GPU system to accelerate three computationally intensive tasks in
medical imaging: training deep neural networks, constructing connectomes from neuroimaging data, and
performing iterative image reconstruction. These tasks are critical to a broad range of NIH-funded research
projects in Yale, all of which would greatly benefit from the proposed system.

title: Hodgkin’s Lymphoma-induced Nephrotic Syndrome
text:
This proposal will explore mechanisms related to the development of glomerular injury and albuminuria in
Hodgkin Lymphoma - induced nephrotic syndrome and includes experiments relevant to new forms of therapy
using cytokine/soluble proteins depletion and/or their receptor blockage.

title: Understanding the Development of Pathogenic CD8 T Cells in HLA-B*27-Associated Acute Anterior Uveitis
text: Uveitis is thought to be promoted by autoreactive T cells and intestinal inflammation, however, whether these factors act together or independently remains unclear. We theorize that a combination of enteric inflammation and cross-reactive CDS T cells leads to the development of HLA-8*27-associated acute anterior uveitis (B27MU), providing a cellular connection between the gut and the eye. We propose to determine the events that programs these CDS T cells to become pathogenic, which will provide a model for understanding the basic biology of other forms of uveitis.

title: Innate allorecognition and KIR/LILR/HLA associations in kidney transplantation
text:
Kidney transplantation is a life-saving treatment for patients with kidney failure. However, long-term survival of
kidney transplants remains suboptimal due to chronic rejection. We propose in this grant application to perform
DNA sequencing of critical regions of the human genome that influence the recipient’s immune response
against the transplanted kidney. Knowledge gained will advance current methods of matching donors to
recipients and improve our understanding of the mechanisms of transplant rejection.

title: Molecular identity of exosomal BK channels
text:
RELEVANCE. Exosomes are potential means of intercellular communications and transmission of
macromolecules between cells, and are projected for drug delivery as well as therapeutic targets for
several diseases including cardioprotection. For the first time, we have discovered and recorded a
functional channel from intact exosomes and showed their potential in cardioprotection. The results of this
investigation will allow the advancement of cardioprotective medicine and provide new molecular targets
in exosomes for therapeutics.
